cards.html: This skill lists the mistakes real teams make with push, and the parts that are outside your control.

1. Using notification messages and expecting your code to run. Symptom: it works in the foreground, but in the background a plain banner appears with none of your logic. Fix: send data messages and build the notification yourself.
  2. Never deleting dead tokens. Symptom: sends slow down, logs fill with UNREGISTERED, and some users get duplicates (old and new install). Fix: delete on that error, and drop tokens on logout.
  3. Treating FCM as guaranteed. Symptom: "I never got it" reports with no trace. Fix: keep the truth in your backend (an inbox or unseen list the app also reads on open). Push only prompts a look.

1. Committing the service-account key. Symptom: a leaked key lets anyone send pushes as you. Fix: keep it out of git, load it from an environment variable or a root-only file, and rotate it if exposed.
  2. A long TTL on time-sensitive messages. Symptom: a "ring" arrives hours later when the phone reconnects. Fix: set TTL to what the message is worth, which is minutes.
  3. Forgetting the notification permission and token refresh. Symptom: new Android users get nothing, and tokens in your table go stale silently. Fix: ask for POST_NOTIFICATIONS at a sensible moment, and re-upload the token whenever the SDK reports a new one and on each login.
1. Stuffing private data or large blobs into the payload. Symptom: you hit the size cap, or leak content to a third party. Fix: send ids and fetch details over your own API.

cards.s: The phone is the hidden tax
cards.html:
• Aggressive battery managers on some phone brands delay or drop pushes for apps that are not whitelisted. You cannot fix this from the server. [consensus]
  • Doze and priority rules mean "high priority" is a privilege. Abuse gets you throttled.
  • The community-maintained site dontkillmyapp.com lists maker-by-maker behaviour. Use it when "it works on my phone" meets "it never arrives on theirs".

• Push only wakes the app. For a live walkie-talkie, the push says "wake up and reconnect", and a socket or WebRTC carries the audio.
  • Ringing via a high-priority push is the standard pattern, but Android adds rules: a full-screen-intent permission, foreground service types, and limits on starting the microphone from the background. These tighten with each Android version. [fast-moving, verify on your target versions]
  • In practice the user usually taps to answer, the app comes to the front, and only then does it start capturing the microphone.
  • Battery cost matters too. A held-open connection is cheap when idle, but the figures depend on the phone and network, so measure on your own devices.

t: The phone is the hidden tax

quiz.q: Your handler never fires in the background. A likely cause?
o: You sent a notification message, not a data message
quiz.why: The OS tray handles notification messages in the background.

quiz.q: Not deleting dead tokens leads to …
o: slower sends and duplicate or wasted work
quiz.why: Clean them when UNREGISTERED comes back.

quiz.q: A service-account key can safely be committed to a private repo.
quiz.why: Keep it out of git; a leaked key lets anyone send pushes as you.

quiz.q: A user on some phone brands never gets your push. The likely reason?
o: An aggressive battery manager delays or drops it
FCM is blocked in their country
quiz.why: You cannot fix this server-side; guide users to whitelist the app.
